# Technical Specification: Advanced BIM-Based Modular Housing System

## 1. System Overview and Material Composition
The modular housing system leverages Building Information Modeling (BIM) methodologies to integrate design, fabrication, and assembly into a streamlined workflow. The primary structural framework is engineered from thin-wall channel steel components, offering an optimal strength-to-weight ratio. This lightweight yet robust material selection enables high-precision off-site manufacturing, reduces transportation costs, and facilitates rapid, standardized assembly on-site.

## 2. Primary Structural Members
The core load-bearing architecture—comprising both vertical structural columns and horizontal transverse beams—utilizes cold-formed C-section steel characterized by inward-bent flanges. Depending on localized load requirements:
* **Single-Section Configuration:** Primary elements utilize standalone C-section profiles with inward flanges for standard load paths.
* **Composite Configuration:** Where enhanced torsional rigidity and axial load capacity are required, components are configured as combined square steel sections. These are formed by oppositely buckling two symmetric C-sections together, creating a closed-profile box column or beam.

## 3. Modular Node Connection Framework
To form a rigid, continuous structural matrix, the system incorporates specialized structural node connectors categorized into three key types:
* **Base Connectors:** Anchor the super-structure securely to the foundational elements.
* **Butting Connectors:** Facilitate linear end-to-end joining of beams and columns to extend structural spans.
* **Crossed Connectors:** Resolve multi-axis intersections, joining vertical columns, horizontal beams, and roof plates at modular grid nodes.

Together, these connectors establish a cohesive structural network capable of efficiently transferring dead and live loads throughout the building envelope.

## 4. Precision Mechanical Interlocking and Fixation
To guarantee precise spatial alignment and superior joint performance without relying solely on traditional welding, the system employs an advanced double-nesting mechanical locking mechanism:

### 4.1 Internal-External Web Nesting
The node connectors feature high-strength webs engineered with strategic inner relief holes. During assembly, the inward-oriented flanges of the C-section steel snap into or buckle directly against these relief holes. This interaction produces a tight internal-external nesting effect, anchoring the connector directly within the core of the steel profile and eliminating internal play.

### 4.2 External Groove Positioning and Anti-Slippage
To reinforce structural stability against shear forces and movement:
* **Concavo-Convex Mating:** The connectors are designed with external positioning grooves that mate directly with corresponding surface contours on the steel components in a male-female (concavo-convex) arrangement.
* **Frictional Locking:** Once nested, the joint assembly is reinforced using high-tensile fastening steel strips. These strips clamp the C-section profiles tightly to the connector, locking the concavo-convex interface in place and completely preventing longitudinal slippage along the channel axis.

## 5. Structural Benefits Summary
By combining BIM-driven manufacturing tolerances with thin-wall C-section geometry and multi-layered mechanical nesting, this modular housing system achieves high dynamic load resistance, minimal structural play, and rapid bolt-and-clamp field assembly. The result is a highly repeatable, safe, and cost-effective construction method optimized for modern industrialized building practices.

# Advanced Interconnection System for Thin-Wall Channel Steel in BIM-Based Modular Housing Construction

## 1. Introduction
The global demand for sustainable, cost-effective, and rapidly deployable infrastructure has accelerated the adoption of modular housing. Among structural materials, cold-formed thin-wall channel steel offers a high strength-to-weight ratio and exceptional versatility. However, traditional connection methods—such as direct field welding or basic angle-plate bolting—often suffer from alignment errors, excessive localized deformation, and labor-intensive assembly processes. To fully realize the efficiency of Building Information Modeling (BIM) workflows and Design for Manufacture and Assembly (DfMA) methodologies, a novel, standardized joint connection system is required. 

This paper outlines a specialized structural joint system that utilizes custom-engineered base, butting, and crossed connectors to transform thin-wall steel modular construction into a precise, high-performance assembly process.

```
       [ Thin-Wall Steel Component ]
                   │
                   ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  SPECIALIZED CONNECTOR SYSTEM   │
  │  • Base                         │
  │  • Butting                      │  ◄── Integrated Features:
  │  • Crossed                      │      • Web Supports
  └─────────────────────────────────┘      • Relief Holes
                   │                       • Positioning Grooves
                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│    CONCAVO-CONVEX NESTING PROCESS   │
│  (Self-Aligning & Friction Locking) │
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
                   │
                   ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────┐
│  HIGH-STRENGTH STANDARDIZED JOINTS  │
│  • Anti-Slippage                    │
│  • Buckling Prevention              │
│  • Full BIM Parametric Compatibility│
└─────────────────────────────────────┘
```

---

## 2. Specialized Connector Architecture
To accommodate the multi-directional load paths inherent in modular steel frameworks, three distinct structural connectors have been developed. Each connector incorporates tailored features designed to work harmoniously with thin-wall channel profiles:

*   **Base Connectors:** Positioned at the primary foundational interface and floor-to-floor module boundaries, these components securely anchor vertical columns, transferring axial and lateral shear loads directly into the substructure.
*   **Butting Connectors:** Designed for inline, end-to-end joining of structural members, these connectors enable seamless extension of beams and columns without sacrificing section modulus or rotational stiffness.
*   **Crossed Connectors:** Engineered for 2D and 3D orthogonal intersections (such as beam-to-column and brace nodes), these units facilitate multi-axis load distribution across complex module geometries.

### Key Integrated Features
Each connector type incorporates three critical engineering features:
1.  **Web Supports:** Internal structural stiffeners designed to reinforce the thin web of the channel steel. By supporting the unreinforced web against localized out-of-plane pressure, these supports prevent web crippling and premature buckling under heavy vertical or lateral loads.
2.  **Relief Holes:** Precision-engineered apertures that mitigate stress concentrations during high-load events. Additionally, these holes absorb minor manufacturing and fabrication tolerances, allowing structural fasteners (such as blind rivets or high-strength bolts) to pass through without distorting the surrounding metal.
3.  **Positioning Grooves:** Recessed tactile keyways stamped directly into the connector body. These act as physical guide tracks that automatically index structural members into their exact coordinates during assembly.

---

## 3. Nesting Mechanics and Assembly Workflow
The system relies on a **concavo-convex nesting geometry**, where the female profile of the thin-wall channel steel mates precisely with the male profile of the connector (or vice versa). 

```
  [Channel Steel Profile]         [Connector Profile]
     ┌───────────┐                   ┌───────────┐
     │  ┌─────┐  │    Concavo-Convex │  ┌─────┐  │
     │  │     │  │   ──────────────> │  │     │  │  ====> Interlocked Joint
     │  └─────┘  │      Nesting      │  └─────┘  │        (Zero Slippage)
     └───────────┘                   └───────────┘
```

### The Assembly Sequence:
1.  **Guided Insertion:** Field workers or robotic assemblers slide the thin-wall channel steel into the connector node. The integrated **positioning grooves** catch the edges of the steel profile, providing a self-aligning mechanism that eliminates the need for manual site measurements.
2.  **Concavo-Convex Engagement:** The interlocking profiles lock together, establishing uniform contact across the entire flange-and-web surface area.
3.  **Fastener Securing:** Pre-drilled pilot holes line up automatically via the relief holes, enabling rapid insertion of self-drilling screws or structural bolts. 

This mechanical arrangement minimizes human error, drastically reduces site assembly time, and creates a clean, flush finish ideal for subsequent wall panels and interior fit-outs.

---

## 4. Structural Performance and Slippage Prevention
A common vulnerability in thin-wall steel structures is joint slippage—the minor longitudinal sliding or rotational displacement at bolt connections caused by dynamic wind loads, seismic events, or live-load movement. 

This connector design neutralizes joint slippage through two primary mechanisms:
*   **Mechanical Interlocking:** The concavo-convex surface profile creates physical shear keys along the connection plane. Force is transferred through direct mechanical bearing across the broad surface area, rather than relying solely on bolt-hole wall friction.
*   **Stress Redistribution:** The embedded **web supports** prevent localized cross-sectional distortion of the channel steel. By maintaining the structural geometry of the steel section under load, the connector prevents the dynamic widening of fastener holes, ensuring long-term joint tightness and overall structural integrity.

The resulting standardized joints possess high moment-resisting capacity, shear strength, and ductility, significantly enhancing the seismic resilience of the entire modular building.

---

## 5. Seamless BIM Integration
By standardizing these connectors into digital dynamic families, the physical connection system aligns directly with BIM software environments (e.g., Autodesk Revit, Tekla Structures). 

*   **Parametric Modeling:** Engineers can instantly populate BIM models with exact geometric representations of base, butting, and crossed connectors.
*   **Automated Clash Detection:** The standardized outer dimensions and pre-calculated relief hole tolerances ensure that structural nodes pass automated clash detection checks during the digital design phase.
*   **Precision Pre-fabrication:** Digital steel cutting schedules generated by the BIM model match the exact indexing locations of the physical positioning grooves, bridging the gap between digital structural design and automated factory fabrication.

---

## 6. Conclusion
The combination of specialized base, butting, and crossed connectors featuring web supports, relief holes, and positioning grooves provides a robust solution for modular steel construction. By replacing modern labor-intensive, error-prone joining techniques with precise concavo-convex nesting, this system achieves high-strength, standardized joints that effectively eliminate structural slippage. Ultimately, this approach enhances structural safety while maximizing the speed, accuracy, and efficiency promised by modern BIM-driven industrial construction.

# SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION

The present disclosure relates generally to prefabricated structural systems, and more particularly to a modular house framing assembly utilizing square steel columns, C-section steel beams, and specialized connection joints incorporating positioning grooves and relief holes for rapid, high-precision assembly and enhanced structural integrity.

### Problem Addressed
Traditional modular steel buildings often suffer from alignment errors during field assembly, high stress concentrations at rigid welded or bolted beam-column nodes, and complex, labor-intensive joint connections. There is a need for a standardized, prefabricated framing system that ensures self-alignment during construction while mitigating structural stress at critical load-bearing joints.

### Summary of the Solution
To overcome the aforementioned limitations, the present disclosure provides a modular structural frame for a building, characterized by an interconnected network of square steel columns and C-section steel beams joined via customized node connectors featuring integrated positioning grooves and stress-relief apertures.

In accordance with one embodiment of the present disclosure, a modular building frame assembly comprises:
*   **At least one column** formed from a square steel hollow section, the column defining a vertical load-bearing axis;
*   **At least one beam** formed from a C-section steel profile, the beam having a web and pair of opposing flanges; and
*   **A joint assembly** configured to operatively couple the at least one column to the at least one beam.

The **joint assembly** comprises a body attached to or integral with an exterior surface of the square steel column. The joint assembly is equipped with **at least one positioning groove** formed along a receiving face thereof. The positioning groove is geometrically complementary to an end portion, lip, or flange of the C-section steel beam. Engagement of the C-section beam within the positioning groove restricts relative rotation and provides positive visual and physical spatial registration (self-alignment) along both vertical and horizontal axes prior to final fastening.

Furthermore, the assembly includes **a plurality of relief holes** strategically disposed at high-stress intersection points, including:
1.  **Corner transitions** of the C-section steel beam ends to prevent stress concentration during bending loads;
2.  **Interface regions** of the joint assembly adjacent to the square steel column to dissipate thermal expansion stresses and localized mechanical strain; and/or
3.  **Access zones** aligned with fastener locations to provide physical clearance for assembly tools, internal utility pass-throughs, or weld-seam relief.

### Key Connection Mechanism
In a preferred embodiment, the connection between the square column and the C-section beam is executed without field welding. The joint assembly is pre-fixed to the square steel column (e.g., via shop welds or high-strength factory bolts). To attach a beam:
1. The end of the C-section beam is guided into the positioning groove of the joint assembly, sliding horizontally or dropping vertically until fully seated.
2. The positioning groove physically captures the C-section beam, maintaining it in a plumb and level orientation.
3. Fasteners (such as structural bolts or rivets) are inserted through pre-aligned mounting holes positioned adjacent to the relief holes.
4. The relief holes prevent localized material tearing or stress concentration around the mechanical fasteners under dynamic wind or seismic loading, while simultaneously serving as clearance pockets for flush-fitting hardware.

### Primary Advantages
The system described herein provides several distinct advantages over the prior art:
*   **Self-Aligning Modular Construction:** The interaction between the positioning grooves and the C-section profiles eliminates the need for manual leveling and clamping during field assembly, significantly reducing construction time and labor costs.
*   **Enhanced Structural Longevity:** The inclusion of relief holes at critical stress nodes redistributes localized forces, preventing micro-cracking and structural fatigue at the column-beam interfaces under cyclic loads.
*   **High Rigidity with Standardized Profiles:** Combining square steel columns (providing superior multi-axis torsional rigidity) with C-section steel beams (providing optimal bending strength-to-weight ratios) optimizes structural performance while utilizing cost-effective, standard steel sections.
*   **Scalability and Modularity:** The standardized joint connections allow for multi-directional extension (X, Y, and Z axes), enabling rapid configuration of single-story or multi-story modular structures.

*It is to be understood that both the foregoing general description and the following detailed description are exemplary and explanatory only and are not restrictive of the disclosure, as claimed.*

**SYSTEM AND CONNECTOR ASSEMBLY FOR QUICK-CONNECT SLIP-RESISTANT JOINING OF THIN-WALLED CHANNEL STEEL IN MODULAR CONSTRUCTION**

---

### **FIELD OF THE INVENTION**
The present invention relates generally to structural connections in modular building construction and, more particularly, to a high-shear, quick-assembly connector assembly configured to join thin-walled cold-formed channel steel members without structural slippage.

---

### **BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION**
Thin-walled channel steel (e.g., C-channels or U-channels) is widely used in modular construction due to its high strength-to-weight ratio. However, conventional connection methods—such as self-tapping screws, standard bolting, or field welding—present significant drawbacks. Screws and standard bolts rely heavily on surface friction, making them prone to shear slippage under lateral and dynamic loads (e.g., wind, seismic, transport forces). Furthermore, thin-wall profiles are susceptible to crushing under high torque, and field welding damages protective galvanized coatings while greatly increasing assembly time. There is a need for a structural connection that eliminates shear slippage while enabling rapid, tool-minimal field assembly.

---

### **SUMMARY OF THE INVENTION**
The present invention solves these technical problems by providing an interlocking connector assembly comprising a pair of opposing mating plates, a integrated micro-serrated friction interface, and a rapid-actuating tensioning clamp. The connector engages pre-formed apertures in the thin-walled steel channels, providing positive mechanical interlocking to prevent linear slippage while simultaneously aligning the structural members.

---

### **DETAILED DESCRIPTION OF PREFERRED EMBODIMENTS**

Referring to the structural components of the assembly:

1. **Interlocking Connector Plates:** The assembly comprises a primary plate and a secondary clamping plate shaped to complementary nest within the internal flange profile of thin-walled channel steel. Each plate includes a plurality of self-locating alignment bosses configured to project through corresponding factory-punched slots in the web of the channel steel.

2. **Anti-Slip Friction Interface:** The face of each plate contacting the steel web features a matrix of hardened micro-serrations or directional teeth. Upon tensioning, these serrations bite into the surface of the channel steel without penetrating the core wall thickness, providing a positive mechanical lock that increases ultimate shear capacity and eliminates directional slippage.

3. **Quick-Lock Tensioning Assembly:** Connecting the plates is a single-action fastener comprising an eccentric cam-lever pin or a single high-shear wedge-bolt. Engaging the quick-lock mechanism applies simultaneous transverse clamping force (pressing the teeth into the steel) and axial drawing force (pulling adjacent modular channel frames flush together).

**Operation:** During modular field assembly, workers align two framing sections, insert the connector assembly into the pre-punched web apertures, and actuate the quick-lock mechanism (e.g., via a 90-degree turn or single impact drive). The alignment bosses ensure instant structural registration, while the micro-serrations lock the connection against shear slippage under load.

---

### **PATENT CLAIMS**

**What is claimed is:**

1. A quick-assembly connector system for joining thin-walled channel steel members in modular buildings, comprising:
   * a first connector plate and a second connector plate configured to clamp opposing sides of at least one thin-walled steel web;
   * a plurality of friction-enhancing projections disposed on a surface of at least one of said connector plates, configured to mechanically engage the thin-walled steel to prevent shear slippage;
   * at least one self-aligning tab projecting from the first connector plate for positioning within a pre-formed aperture of the channel steel; and
   * a quick-actuating tensioning mechanism extending through the plates, operable to transition the assembly from a loose alignment state to a fully locked, slip-resistant clamped state in a single mechanical motion.

2. The connector system of claim 1, wherein the quick-actuating tensioning mechanism comprises an eccentric cam mechanism configured to apply both axial clamping force and lateral drawing force simultaneously.

A **BIM-Based Modular House** represents the intersection of digital technology and advanced manufacturing in the construction industry. By combining **Building Information Modeling (BIM)** with **Modular/Off-Site Construction**, houses are designed, simulated, and engineered digitally down to the millimeter before being manufactured in a factory and assembled on-site.

Here is a comprehensive breakdown of how BIM-based modular housing works, its benefits, workflow, and future potential.

---

### 1. What is the Core Concept?

*   **Modular Housing:** Buildings constructed off-site in standardized volumetric sections (modules) inside a controlled factory, then transported to the site and assembled.
*   **BIM (Building Information Modeling):** A 3D digital representation of a facility’s physical and functional characteristics, containing detailed data about every component (structural, MEP, architectural).
*   **The Synergy (DfMA):** Modular housing requires extreme precision—if a module is off by 5mm, it won't fit on-site. BIM enables **Design for Manufacture and Assembly (DfMA)**, ensuring zero errors when transitioning from digital designs to factory production lines.

---

### 2. Step-by-Step Workflow

```
[ BIM Design & DfMA ] ➔ [ Virtual Stress & Clash Test ] ➔ [ CAM Factory Fabrication ] ➔ [ Site Assembly ] ➔ [ Digital Twin Handover ]
```

#### Phase 1: Digital Design & DfMA (Design for Manufacture and Assembly)
*   **Parametric Modeling:** Architects use BIM tools (like Autodesk Revit, Graphisoft Archicad) to create parametric modular components (walls, MEP pods, structural frames).
*   **Transport Constraints:** Module dimensions are programmed into BIM based on local road transport limits (e.g., maximum height, width, and weight).

#### Phase 2: Virtual Pre-construction (Clash Detection & LOD 400)
*   **High Level of Detail (LOD 400/500):** The model includes exact fabrication details—every bolt, weld, electrical conduit, and pipe joint.
*   **Clash Detection:** Automated checks ensure plumbing pipes don't intersect with steel beams, preventing costly factory rework.

#### Phase 3: Automated Manufacturing (CAM)
*   **Direct-to-Fabrication:** BIM data is exported directly to **Computer-Aided Manufacturing (CAM)** software.
*   **Robotic Fabrication:** CNC machines, light-gauge steel roll-formers, and robotic welders cut and assemble frames directly from the BIM file.

#### Phase 4: Logistics and On-Site Assembly
*   **Sequence Simulation (4D BIM):** The BIM model simulates the exact sequence of crane lifting, truck arrivals, and module placement.
*   **Rapid Installation:** Foundation work (done on-site) and module fabrication (done in the factory) happen simultaneously. Assembly usually takes **1 to 5 days**.

#### Phase 5: Facility Management (7D BIM)
*   The owner receives a **Digital Twin**—a live digital model containing warranties, pipe locations, structural details, and maintenance schedules embedded in every digital element.

---

### 3. Key Benefits of BIM-Driven Modular Homes

| Feature | Traditional Construction | BIM Modular Construction |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Construction Time** | 8 – 18 months | **2 – 4 months** (50%–70% faster) |
| **Quality Control** | Dependent on weather & site labor | **Factory precision** ($\pm 1 \text{ mm}$ tolerance) |
| **Material Waste** | High (~10–15% waste) | **Near zero** (<2% waste due to exact BIM cutting lists) |
| **Safety** | High-risk outdoor site work | **Safe, controlled factory environment** |
| **Cost Predictability** | Unpredictable (rework, delays) | **High predictability** (exact cost modeled upfront) |

---

### 4. How BIM Dimensions (3D to 7D) Apply to Modular Homes

1.  **3D (Geometry):** Exact 3D volumetric design, MEP coordination, and structural layouts.
2.  **4D (Time):** Timeline integration. Tracks module manufacturing schedules and crane assembly logistics on-site.
3.  **5D (Cost):** Real-time estimation. As you add a modular wall in BIM, the exact cost update includes factory labor, material, and transport.
4.  **6D (Sustainability):** Energy performance analysis, carbon footprint tracking, and material lifecycle assessment.
5.  **7D (Operations):** Long-term maintenance. Homeowners know exact model numbers of in-wall plumbing without breaking walls.

---

### 5. Technical Stack for BIM Modular Projects

*   **Architectural/Structural BIM:** Autodesk Revit, Tekla Structures, ARCHICAD.
*   **DFMA & Fabrication:** Autodesk Inventor, SolidWorks (for detailed manufacturing output), Dassault Systèmes CATIA.
*   **Clash Detection & Coordination:** Navisworks, Solibri.
*   **4D/5D Simulation:** Synchro 4D, CostX.
*   **Machine Integration:** IFC (Industry Foundation Classes) and BVBS files directly fed into CNC machinery.

---

### 6. Challenges and Solutions

*   **Challenge:** High initial upfront cost for software, templates, and factory setup.
    *   *Solution:* Standardization. Creating modular BIM libraries that can be reused across hundreds of home configurations.
*   **Challenge:** Inflexible late-stage design changes.
    *   *Solution:* VR/AR walkthroughs built from the BIM model allow clients to finalize designs before manufacturing begins.
*   **Challenge:** Tolerances between factory modules and site foundations.
    *   *Solution:* Using **3D Laser Scanning** on-site to verify foundation accuracy before transporting the modules.

---

### 7. Future Trends

*   **Generative AI + BIM:** AI algorithms automatically generating optimal modular layouts based on local zoning codes, sunlight, and factory material limits.
*   **IoT Smart Modules:** Embedding smart sensors into modular panels during factory production, connected directly to the BIM model for real-time structural health monitoring.
*   **Circular Economy / Deconstructable Modules:** Homes designed via BIM to be disassembled and relocated or recycled at the end of their lifecycle.
